meta.what: A deliberately small, cited set of notes for readings whose use depends on context. Each use names where it applies. None of these is a universal English meaning, and none is a translation of a particular line.

baplar.title: SOAS, Babylonian and Assyrian Poetry and Literature: An Archive of Recordings (BAPLAR)

DIŠ.summary: The sign of a single vertical wedge. What it stands for depends on where it is written.

uses.context: At the start of a line in omen collections
uses.use: read šumma, Akkadian ‘if’, opening the observed sign (the protasis). Borger marks this equation with a query and notes that some editors transliterate it as ¶.
the numeral 1 (also 60 in the sexagesimal system)
a determinative (unpronounced classifier) marking a, usually male, personal name; transliterated {m} or {I} when used this way
the Akkadian preposition ana ‘to, for’ (the release’s sign layer writes ana with the same sign, ABZ 480)

DIŠ.caution: Capitals give the sign name; the source translation, where present, gives the editor’s contextual rendering.

logogram.text: Written in capitals: a logogram, a sign used for a whole word. Its Akkadian reading is usually a different word from the sign name (KUR can stand for mātu ‘land’). Capitals mark the sign; they do not spell the spoken word.

syllabic.text: Lower case: a sound value of a sign, usually one syllable of a word that is split across several signs with hyphens (a-na).

subindex.text: Subscript numbers tell apart different signs with the same sound value (du, du₂, du₃ are three signs). ₓ means a value whose sign number is not settled.

determinative.text: Curly braces mark a determinative, an unpronounced classifier: {d} before a god's name, {ki} after a place, {m} before a man's name.

flags.text: # damaged, ? uncertain, ! corrected by the editor, [ ] broken away, x an unreadable sign. These describe the tablet and the edition, not the word.

number.text: A number. Cuneiform counts in base 60, and the same wedge can mean 1 or 60.

recordings.note: Linked only when the source's own genre names the composition. A recording is a modern scholar reading another manuscript or edition of the same composition, not this tablet.

pronunciation.label: Reading & pronunciation
points: A transliteration names the signs as they are written; it is not a spelling of how the words sounded. Scholars write a separate normalized (transcribed) form for that, for example šumma for the word written DIŠ in omens.
A logogram is read as an Akkadian word that can be unrelated to its sign name: KUR is read mātu ‘land’ (among other words).
Normalized forms are modern scholarly reconstructions. The exact ancient sound is not known, and it varied by period and region; this workbench does not generate audio.
Modern Assyriologists have recorded readings of literary texts in normalized Akkadian (SOAS BAPLAR). They show one scholar's informed reading, not an ancient voice.
